From An Owl
(the last of a continuing series)
JL here is a special nostalgic pleasure for
me in preparing my last "From An Owl.
"
Six years ago, when my tenure as Pres
ident ofthe Executive Council began, Psi
Upsilon embarked upon an ambitious
program to expand its services to chap
ters and alumni organizations, to increase
the number of chapters, and to instill in
new and exciting ways the sense of broth
erhood and service to school and nation
that we inherited from our Founders over
150 years ago.
Much has happened since then! In our
efforts, we have:
(1) Developed and implemented an in
ternational program of general liability
insurance for all of our chapters and
alumni organizations, making this insur
ance available for the first time to a num
ber of chapters and minimizing the in
creasing costs of insurance premiums by
spreading the costs over multiple years.
(2) Developed and implemented, in
cooperation with the Psi Upsilon Foun
dation, the first Psi Upsilon Leadership
Institute aimed at focusing the attention
of our undergraduate leaders on the crit
ical responsibilities that they face in each
of their chapters. A measure of the
strength of this program was recognized
in the recent award to Psi Upsilon by the
National Interfraternity Conference!
(3) Added four new chapters and pro
visional chapters (Kappa Phi at Penn
State, Upsilon Tau at the University of
Texas, Beta Alpha at Miami University
of Ohio, and the Beta Kappa at Wash
ington State University) and reactivated
three chapters (Sigma at Brown, Epsilon
at the University of California at Berke
ley, and Mu at Minnesota) �
more chap
ters than during any comparable six year
period in our history!
(4) Developed and implemented a Risk
Management Program which, in spite of
the challenges it has presented to every
one involved in the process, has provided
a sound basis for accentuating the posi
tive aspects of fraternity life and elimi
nating the negatives that have achieved
so much nationwide media attention in
recent years.
This progress, although it has occurred
during the past six years, has been pos
sible because of the tremendous efforts
of so many brothers �
Psi U and inter
fraternal, spouses, educators and admin
istrators. The list is far too long for me
to include everyone, but some are due
special mention for their untiring efforts:
Chuck Hall, Nu Alpha '71, my successor,
who has supervised the financial affairs
of the Fraternity for five of these years
and truly made the term "doing more
with less
"
meaningful; David Brown, Ep
silon Phi '66, who has served as a Vice
President or the \'ice President of the
Executive Council during this entire pe
riod and has been both the "conscience"
and the "conciliator" of the Executive
Council; John Menzies, Pi '41, who has
served as Secretary of the Executive
Council during five of these years as well
as Chairman of the Nominating Com
mittee and has brought a refreshing sense
of devotion to the concept that new gen
erations must assume responsibility for
leadership in the Fraternity, These three
brothers served with me as members of
the Executive Committee and truly pro
vided the first "collective leadership
"
in
a meaningful sense that the Fraternity
has seen. To each of them I and the Fra
ternity owe a tremendous debt of grati
tude.
During this same six years, Psi U has
not been spared its share of misfortunes,
better known as challenges not met or
opportunities not taken. Perhaps the most
distressing of these misfortunes has been
the loss to inactive status of three of our
most revered chapters: the Rho at Wis
consin, the Delta at New York Univer
sity, and the Tau at Penn �
the first to
undergraduate apathy and the latter two
to undergraduate activities seriously of
fensive to alumni, administrators, and the
International Fraternity alike. The sig
nificant efforts of the alumni organiza
tions in all three instances will assure that
these chapters do not remain long on the
inactive roles but will return to their for
mer positions of leadership in the Fra
ternity,
It has been my privilege during these
six years to serve with four Executive
Director/Vice Presidents of the Frater
nity�Henry B, Poor, Gamma '39 (19841987); Kathleen M, McGlone, Lambda
'82H (1987-1989); Thomas L, Phillips,
Omicron '85 (Acting, 1989-1990); and
Mark A, Williams, Phi '76 (1990-present
and future!), I should not wish that any
future President of the Executive Coun
cil should have the opportunity again to
serve with this many Chief Administra
tive Officers! Were it not for the high
quality of each of these individuals, an
other President might have been consid
ered slightly daft to attempt such a series
of working relationships.
In spite ofthe horrible tragedy that the
death of Kathy McGlone created for all
who knew her, I am sure she would be
proud of the opportunities for new prog
ress and growth that her passing in
spired. Her gentle nature, her endless
demonstrations of brotherhood in its old
est and truest meaning, and her personal
warmth and strength were not lost on the
thousands of Psi Us and others with whom
she came in contact,
I cannot say "goodbye" without look
ing happily and enthusiastically to the
future. I know that Chuck Hall and Mark
Williams shared my sincere excitement
about bringing three new provisional
chapters/colonies into the Fraternity in
just one month (September) of this year
and that they will bring those groups into
full chapter status as soon as they are
eligible. Psi U will expand to other cam
puses where fraternities can be appre
ciated and nurtured not only by under
graduates and alumni but also by
administrators. At the same time, we must
continue to face to the last ounce of
strength the challenges to fraternity ex
istence that are occurring on more and
more
campuses where we have chapters
�
where schools will not allow freedom
to choose any fraternity much less free
dom of association. We must continue to
strive for the attainment of those goals
for which we were founded �
the high
est intellectual, moral and social excel
lence �
through greater educational ef
forts of all kinds at the chapter level,
through expanded nationwide and re
gional Leadership Institutes for under
graduate and alumni leaders, and through
the day-to-day examples that our alumni
set for our
undergraduates. We are a
proud Fraternity with a proud history �
let us never forget why we are proud and
that maintaining that pride requires our
eternal vigilance and constant efforts,
I thank each and every one of you for
giving me the opportunity to serve you
during these last six years, I shall cer
tainly never forget them, but , , , then
again, I don't intend to exactly disappear
either!
Yours in the Bonds,
William R. Robie

Mu Chapter Celebrates Revitalization
(Minneapolis, MN) On October 25, 1990, approximately 100 alumni attended
a grand reopening celebration at the Mu Chapter House adjacent to the campus
of the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. The celebration was the cul
mination of three years of hard work by the alumni board and fund raising
committee which resulted in a
complete renovation of the chapter house. The
total cost of the renovation, including fund raising and retirement of past ob
ligations, was $450,000,00, To date, over $300,000,00 has been pledged to the
effort.
During the summer of 1990, the chapter house was completely gutted and
rebuilt. Included in the renovation effort were the construction of brand new
rooms with built-in beds, study areas, phone jacks and up-to-date electrical
systems. The entire plumbing system was replaced, and brand new bathrooms
and showers installed on all three floors. The common areas ofthe house such
as the living room, kitchen, card room, and hallways were completely redone.
At this time the Mu chapter house is among the nicest fraternity houses on the
University of Minnesota campus.
In conjunction with the physical renovation efforts, the alumni made a decision
to revitalize the undergraduate chapter as well. During the fall of 1989, the
undergraduate chapter was declared inactive. During the summer of 1990, the
alumni conducted a rush program for new members. Two of the former un
dergraduate members, Todd Knutson and Mike Midlestadt, petitioned for readmission and their petitions were
accepted by the board. In addition, six brand
new undergraduates were initiated on October 24, 1990,
The renovation, rejuvenation of the undergraduate chapter, and the grand
opening received considerable attention in the University of Minnesota com
munity. While other local fraternities have considered badly needed renovations
of their chapter houses, the Mu Chapter is the only fraternity thus far to have
accomplished the goal. The Mu Chapter alumni are congratulated for assuming
a leadership role and insuring a long and successful future for Psi Upsilon at
the University of Minnesota,

RISK NO MORE
(New Orleans, LA) At the recent meeting
of the National Interfraternity Confer
ence, the risk management standards of
the Fraternity Insurance Purchasing
Group were adopted as the risk manage
ment standards of the NIC. The NIC is
the umbrella organization for 62 national
and international fraternities. The adop
tion of these standards moves the frater
nity world one step closer to having a
mandatory risk management policy for all
fraternity chapters,
Psi Upsilon has been a member of the
Fraternity Insurance Purchasing Group
since 1988, and has been pushing our
chapters into compliance with these im
portant standards which address the key
issues facing fraternities, namely alcohol
abuse, hazing, and sexual harassment.
While the implementation of these
standards has been somewhat controver
sial, those chapters that have come into
compliance have done so with tremen
dous success on their campuses.

SPEAKING OF
THE FOUNDATION
The First Thirty Years (continued)
Now it was 1987. In the first five installments of this column we
have endeavored to describe the 1958 inception of The Psi Upsilon
Foundation, Inc., its modest role for more than two decades, the
Sesquicentennial Fund program mounted in 1981-82, early returns
of highly gratifying proportions, and adjustments fashioned to assist
individual Chapters with pressing needs.
Just how well had we done by 1987? Confirmed pledges of nearly
$1,250,000 had been received at the time of our annual Foundation
meeting that April, with almost $500,000 of this total already paid
in. Compare this with the Foundation's total corpus of just over
$300,000 prior to the Sesquicentennial Fund's start. To some this
represented a signal achievement; to others the potential had barely
been tapped. Because the operation was unique, in reality there
was no measuring stick by which to gauge its success.
Astonishing, however, was the fact that this pledge total had been
achieved by just sixty-five participants! They pledged an incredible
average of over $19,000 each. What a remarkable expression ofthe
loyalty of Psi U alumni and of their firm belief in the continuing
value of undergraduate membership in our great Fraternity!
The entire approach during these five-and-a-half years had been
by personal one-to-one contact. None of the standard fund-raising
techniques had been followed. There were no volunteer commit
tees, no glittering brochures, no broad-based mailings. The Ses
quicentennial Fund program had not even been announced publicly
with fanfare.
And it still has not today! With the active involvement of our
professional fund-raising consultant, one or two of us had traveled
the length and breadth of the land, visiting alumni whom we be
lieved to be in a position to support the program substantially if
they so chose. Oftentimes we made a number of visits to targeted
alumni. We weren't always successful in securing a pledge, of course.
But without exception we were warmly received always. Our pride
in being members of this Fraternity grew apace.
As we approached this 1987 milestone it became increasingly clear
that the future of Psi Upsilon was inextricably interwoven with the
strength ofthe Foundation. Costs of operation were escalating more
rapidly than the growth of the Annual Giving program, a critical
income source for the Fraternity. Scholarship grants needed to be
increased, as more and more undergraduates were experiencing
difficulty in meeting college expenses. And the stresses to which
today's generation of students were being subjected called for new
programs which the Fraternity's budget could no longer absorb.
The solution? Separate the functions of the Foundation from the
Fraternity, so that greater emphasis could be given to Foundation
operations. This was the decision of the Fraternity's Executive
Council, endorsed by the Foundation's Board of Directors at its
annual meeting in April, 1987.
Thus commenced a new chapter in the chronicle of the Foun
dation. Did this change accomplish its purpose? How about the
cooperative Chapter programs described in our last edition? See
the next issue.
Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39
Foundation Executive Director

ARE WE who we say WE ARE?
(Atlanta, GA) In 100 degree plus weather, the first Psi Upsilon Leadership
Institute and the 147th Psi Upsilon Convention were held at the beautiful RitzCarlton, Buckhead. Four days of activities began on Thursday, August 21 when

The Leadership Institute began with a staged mock trial on Thursday evening
and ended with a motivational address on Saturday. In between, the attendees
broke into small groups of seven undergraduates each, with an alumnus serving
as facilitator. These groups had in-depth discussions on such issues as: members
not paying dues, the role of fraternity ritual, alcohol use and abuse, pledge
education and hazing, and many other important topics.
The 147th Convention began on Saturday, August 23 with over 100 delegates
and guests in attendance. One particularly important piece of legislation was
the creation of the Court of Brotherhood. "This proposed amendment to the Psi
Upsilon Constitution creates a judicial branch of the fraternity. The proposal
was adopted as an interim measure so that the 148th Convention could refine
it.
Saturday evening was the formal convention banquet, hosted by the Gamma
Tau Chapter at the Georgia Institute of Technology. William R. Robie, Epsilon

service as President. Charles M. Hall, Nu Alpha '74, Treasurer ofthe Executive

Thomas J. Watson

father and son �
ran IBM for nearly
sixty years. Thomas
Senior joined IBM
before it had its pres
ent name, when it was
a small struggling
manufacturer of tab
ulating equipment,
time clocks, and and
meat scales. A selfmade man, Tom, Sr,
began as an itinerant
salesman of sewing
machines, and learned
his management les
sons at the knee of
John Patterson, leg
endary founder of the
National Cash Regis
ter Company, The highest paid and the most celebrated
CEO in pre-World War II America, he put IBM on the
map. His son, Tom, Jr. , took over the company from his
father in 1956 and put IBM into the computer business
so
completely and so
successfully that to millions around
the world IBM means computers. Under his fifteen-year
leadership IBM enjoyed the most spectacular burst of
growth in business history, becoming a hugely profitable
$7,5 billion-a-year enterprise.
That very public story of how Thomas J, Watson, Jr,
became as Fortune Magazine dubbed him, "the most suc
cessful capitahst in history," is intimately recounted in
FATHER, SON & CO.: My Life at IBM and Beyond. But
also revealed is the very private story of why the author
was so driven to succeed. The dominant theme in the book
is Watson's intense relationship with his father. Writing
with candor and self-deprecating humor Watson comes to
grips with his love for and rivalry with "the old gendeman"
who shaped him, as well as with his close and tempestuous
attachment to his brother, Dick, who ran the IBM inter
national division. World Trade.
Thomas Watson, Jr. ,
the inspiration for future genera
tions of undergraduates and business school students, was
so unmotivated at Brown University he barely graduated.
He writes that "I was totally qualified to be either a playboy
or an
airplane bum." It was that affinity for flying that
earned Watson his first distinction in life. He joined the
Air Force as a pilot in World War II, rising to the rank of
lieutenant colonel, and was sent to Russia to help set up
America's Lend-Lease program.
When the war ended, he beheved himself ready to as
sume the responsibility at IBM he had so studiously
avoided. Under the charismatic leadership of his father,
IBM had boomed during the war years. Brother Watson
recalls his long struggle at IBM headquarters to convince
his father that he was a worthy successor. "During the ten
years after World War II, Father taught me his business
secrets as we worked together. It was a stormy relation
ship. In public he would praise me lavishly, and I'd hear
from other people the nice things he was saying about my
shrewdness and brains and talent as a manager. But in
private Father and I had terrible fights that led us again
and again to the brink of estrangement. These arguments
would frequently end in tears, me in tears and Dad in
tears."
While the family bonds that tied Watson to his entire
clan of parents, siblings, wife and children were deep and
strong, he and his father "fought about every major issue
of the business �
how to finance IBM's growth, whether
to settle or fight a federal anti-trust suit, what role in IBM
other members of our family ought to play.
"
When the author finally was named CEO of the com
pany in 1956 by his father, six weeks before the latter's
death, he was determined to push IBM into computers as
fast as possible �
"one of the things on which we never
saw
eye-to-eye."
Watson details the battles both behind-the-scenes within
IBM and in the open marketplace that led to IBM's su
premacy. He tells the inside story of the creation of the
IBM System/360, which ultimately became the computer
system, launched in 1964, that transformed the industry

Obituaries
John F. Bush, Jr., Upsilon '22, died
at the age of 89 on October 9, 1990, With
his death Psi Upsilon has lost one of its
most loyal sons. Throughout his life.
Brother Bush devoted himself to his fam
ily, to the Episcopal Church, and to qual
ity education, especially among the
members of the Upsilon Chapter of Psi
Upsilon.
He was a longtime member of the
Board of Trustees of Psi Upsilon Alumni
Association of Western New York, Inc.
serving as its treasurer and twice as pres
ident. He was treasurer of the campaign
which raised funds to build the Upsilon
Chapter House on the River Campus of
the University of Rochester in 1930. In
1959, he was elected to the Executive
Council of the Psi Upsilon International
Fratemity and served actively for many
years.
Among his many activities were serv
ice as director of the Legal Aid Society
and Travelers Aid, a trustee of the Al
lendale School in Rochester, a member
of the Alumni Council of the University
of Rochester, and Vestryman, Warden,
Development Fund Treasurer, and Fi
nance Committee Chairman of Christ
Episcopal Church in Pittsford, New York.
Brother Bush was an exceptionally suc
cessful businessman. Upon his gradua
tion from the University of Rochester he
spent eight years in the advertising agency
business, first with Lyddon & Hanford
Company and later as a co-founder and
officer of Hughes Wolff & Company. In
1930 he joined the Puritan Company, Inc.
and served it and its manufacturing sub
sidiary, Genesee Research Corporation,
as General Manager and President until
1954 when they merged the companies
with Olin Mathieson Chemical Corpo
ration.
Brother Bush retired from active busi
ness in 1956 and divided his time be
tween business interests, education, and
writing. He was a part-time member of
the faculty of the University of Roches
ter's School of Business Administration,
Chairman of the Rochester Research and
Development syndicate (a venture cap
ital group), and also helped promote an
early career development program at the
University of Rochester which helped
undergraduate students establish con
tacts with members ofthe business com
munity in their chosen areas of study and
interest.
Upon his retirement. Brother Bush also
established a Scholarship Fund to benefit
members and potential members of the
'
Upsilon who, without the helping hand
of a brother, might not be able to benefit
from the challenges and experiences af
forded by membership in Psi Upsilon.
Over the years, this fund has provided a
helping hand to numerous undergradutes. It continues to serve this same
mission today under the auspices of the
financial aid program of the University of
Rochester as the John F. Bush Scholar
ship Fund.
John F. Bush, Jr, is survived by his
wife Elizabeth Daly Bush, his son John
F, Bush, III, his daughter Mrs. Richard
J. Garrett, a niece, and two granddaugh
ters.
F. Ryan Duffy, Jr., Rho '43, died No
vember 16 in his home after a long ill
ness. Brother Duffy had been Circuit
Judge from 1961 to 1971 and had been a
lawyer in private practice in Milwaukee.
Samuel S. Stratton, Upsilon '37, passed
away on September 13 after a massive
heart attack. He was 73. Brother Stratton
had been a 15-term New York congress
man until 1988 when he retired. A Dem
ocrat who was strong on national defense.
Brother Stratton supported proposed in
creases in defense spending and new
weapons systems, but also voted for such
"liberal' issues as a national minimum
welfare payment and for economic sanc
tions against South Africa. At the 1983
Psi Upsilon Sesquicentennial celebration
at Union College, Brother Stratton pro
cured a flag that had flown over the U.S.
Capitol which he presented to be flown
from the Psi Upsilon flagpole at Union
College.

Six years ago, when my tenure as Pres

ters and alumni organizations, to increase

erhood and service to school and nation

Much has happened since then! In our

ternational program of general liability
insurance for all of our chapters and
alumni organizations, making this insur
ance available for the first time to a num
ber of chapters and minimizing the in
creasing costs of insurance premiums by
spreading the costs over multiple years.
(2) Developed and implemented, in
cooperation with the Psi Upsilon Foun
dation, the first Psi Upsilon Leadership
Institute aimed at focusing the attention
of our undergraduate leaders on the crit
ical responsibilities that they face in each
of their chapters. A measure of the
strength of this program was recognized
in the recent award to Psi Upsilon by the
National Interfraternity Conference!
(3) Added four new chapters and pro
visional chapters (Kappa Phi at Penn
State, Upsilon Tau at the University of
Texas, Beta Alpha at Miami University
of Ohio, and the Beta Kappa at Wash
ington State University) and reactivated
three chapters (Sigma at Brown, Epsilon
at the University of California at Berke
ley, and Mu at Minnesota) �
more chap
ters than during any comparable six year

Management Program which, in spite of

a sound basis for accentuating the posi
tive aspects of fraternity life and elimi
nating the negatives that have achieved
so much nationwide media attention in
recent years.

Psi U and inter

istrators. The list is far too long for me

The First Thirty Years (continued)
Now it was 1987. In the first five installments of this column we
have endeavored to describe the 1958 inception of The Psi Upsilon
foundation, Inc., its modest role for more than two decades, the
Sesquicentennial Fund program mounted in 1981-82, early returns
ot highly gratifying proportions, and adjustments fashioned to assist
individual Chapters with pressing needs.
�i^o^n A^"^ r""^' ^^^ "^^ ^"""^ ^y ^^^'^- Confirmed pledges of nearly
!(. 1,250, 000 had been received at the time of our annual Foundation
meeting that April, with almost $500,000 of this total already paid
in.
Compare this with the Foundation's total corpus of just over
$300,000 prior to the Sesquicentennial Fund's start. To some this
represented a
signal achievement; to others the potential had barely
been tapped. Because the operation was unique, in reality there
was no
measuring stick by which to gauge its success.
Astonishing, however, was the fact that this pledge total had been
achieved by just sixty-five participants! They pledged an incredible
average of over $19,000 each. What a remarkable expression ofthe
loyalty of Psi U alumni and of their firm belief in the continuing
value of undergraduate membership in our great Fraternity!
The entire approach during these five-and-a-half years had been
by personal one-to-one contact. None of the standard fund-raising
techniques had been followed. There were no volunteer commit
tees, no
glittering brochures, no broad-based mailings. The Ses
quicentennial Fund program had not even been announced publicly
with fanfare.
And it still has not today! "With the active involvement of our
professional fund-raising consultant, one or two of us had traveled
the length and breadth of the land, visiting alumni whom we be
lieved to be in a position to support the program substantially if
they so chose. Oftentimes we made a number of visits to targeted
alumni. We weren't always successful in securing a pledge, of course.
But without exception we were warmly received always. Our pride
in being members of this Fraternity grew apace.
As we approached this 1987 milestone it became increasingly clear
that the future of Psi Upsilon was inextricably interwoven with the
strength ofthe Foundation. Costs of operation were
escalating more
rapidly than the growth of the Annual Giving program, a critical
income source for the Fraternity. Scholarship grants needed to be
increased, as more and more undergraduates were
experiencing
difficulty in meeting college expenses. And the stresses to which
today's generation of students were being subjected called for new
programs which the Fraternity's budget could no longer absorb.
The solution? Separate the functions ofthe Foundation from the
Fraternity, so that greater emphasis could be given to Foundation
operations. This was the decision of the Fraternity's Executive
Council, endorsed by the Foundation's Board of Directors at its
annual meeting in April, 1987.
Thus commenced a new chapter in the chronicle of the Foun
dation. Did this change accomphsh its purpose? How about the
cooperative Chapter programs described in our last edition? See
the next issue.

and members of the Tau Chapter were

verse. Not all fraternities at Penn are.

The Leadership Institute began with a staged mock trial on Thursday evening
and ended with a motivational address on Saturday. In between, the attendees
broke into small groups of seven undergraduates each, with an alumnus serving
as facihtator. These groups had in-depth discussions on such issues as: meinbers
not paying dues, the role of fraternity ritual, alcohol use and abuse, pledge
education and hazing, and many other important topics.
The 147th Convention began on Saturday, August 23 with over 100 delegates
and guests in attendance. One particularly important piece of legislation was
the creation of the Court of Brotherhood. This proposed amendment to the Psi
Upsilon Constitution creates a judicial branch of the fraternity. The proposal
was adopted as an interim measure so that the 148th Convention could refine
it.
